title: AI Is Rewriting the Rules of Entertainment in 2026 — And Nobody Can Agree If That's a Good Thing
author: HedwigPost Editorial
excerpt: Artificial intelligence is transforming how movies are made, music is composed, and content is recommended. Here is how AI is reshaping entertainment in 2026 — and what it means for artists, studios, and viewers.
content:
The Revolution Is Already Happening

When the 2023 Hollywood writers' and actors' strikes placed AI at the centre of the most significant labour dispute the entertainment industry had seen in decades, many observers assumed the debate would resolve cleanly — either AI would be limited by contract or it would be unleashed. The reality of 2026 is, predictably, messier and more interesting than either extreme. AI has become deeply embedded in the entertainment industry's production infrastructure, its marketing, its content recommendation systems, and increasingly its creative process itself. And the industry is still actively negotiating what that means for the humans at its centre.

A landmark WrapPRO research report published in January 2026 identified AI integration as the single most defining trend in the entertainment industry this year. "Breakthroughs in generative video are transforming production workflows," the report found, "even as audiences and creatives remain uneasy about authenticity, labor impacts, and AI's environmental footprint." That tension — between the efficiency AI offers and the humanity it potentially displaces — is the defining story of entertainment in 2026.

How Studios Are Using AI Right Now

The most widespread current application of AI in Hollywood is in pre-production and post-production workflows. AI tools are being used to generate concept art and storyboards at a fraction of traditional cost. Visual effects studios are using AI-powered compositing and de-aging tools that would have required hundreds of hours of human VFX work five years ago. AI dubbing and lip-sync technology — which can translate an actor's dialogue into any language while maintaining the appearance of speaking that language naturally — is transforming how global content is distributed, with Netflix reporting that AI-dubbed content has significantly higher completion rates than subtitle-only versions in non-English-speaking markets including India.

In music, AI composition tools are now routinely used in the production of film scores, advertising music, and streaming playlist content. The controversy over AI-generated music that mimics specific artists' vocal styles has prompted several high-profile legal challenges. In March 2026, the US Copyright Office released updated guidance on AI-generated content — determining that works created entirely by AI are not eligible for copyright protection, but that human-AI collaborative works may qualify depending on the degree of human creative input.

The Creator Economy and AI: Threat or Tool?

For independent content creators — YouTubers, podcasters, Instagramers, and TikTok creators — AI presents a more ambiguous picture. On one hand, AI tools dramatically lower the cost of producing high-quality content: AI can write scripts, edit video, generate thumbnails, and optimise posting schedules. Creators who once needed teams to compete with major studios can now produce professional-quality content solo. On the other hand, the same AI tools that empower individual creators also enable the mass production of AI-generated content that floods platforms, making it harder for any individual creator to stand out.

The WrapPRO report identifies the "dissolution of boundaries between Hollywood and the creator economy" as one of the six key trends defining 2026, noting that studios are increasingly working with YouTube and TikTok creators as both marketers and talent, while social platforms are professionalising and moving into the living room through smart TV apps.

What AI in Entertainment Means for Viewers in India

Indian viewers are experiencing AI's entertainment impact primarily through two channels: personalised content recommendation (Netflix and Amazon Prime's AI-driven "what to watch next" engines are becoming increasingly accurate at predicting Indian viewing preferences across languages and genres) and AI dubbing of Korean and Western content into Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, and other Indian languages, dramatically expanding the addressable audience for global content. For Indian fans of K-pop, K-drama, and Hollywood films, AI dubbing means more content in local languages than ever before — a genuine quality-of-experience improvement. title: "Michael" Biopic 2026: Jaafar Jackson Steps Into His Uncle's Shoes — Everything We Know Before the April 24 Release
author: HedwigPost Editorial
excerpt: The Michael Jackson biopic starring his nephew Jaafar Jackson releases on April 24, 2026. Here is everything we know — the casting, the controversy, the music, and whether this film can do justice to the King of Pop.
content:
The Most Anticipated Biopic of the Decade

On April 24, 2026, one of the most anticipated and debated films in recent Hollywood history will finally reach cinema screens worldwide. Michael, the authorised biographical film about the life of Michael Jackson — the King of Pop and the bestselling solo music artist in history — stars Jaafar Jackson, the late star's nephew, in the title role. Directed by Antoine Fuqua (Training Day, The Equalizer) and produced with the cooperation of the Jackson Estate, the film promises an unprecedented level of access to archival footage, personal testimony, and the musical catalogue that defined the second half of the 20th century.

The casting of Jaafar Jackson is the film's most talked-about creative decision. At 23, Jaafar has spent years immersed in his uncle's music and performance style. Screen test footage released by the production company shows an extraordinary physical and vocal resemblance that goes far beyond superficial mimicry — a genuine absorption of movement, presence, and musical sensibility. Early industry viewers who have seen portions of the film report that Jaafar's performance is genuinely startling in its authenticity.

What Does the Film Cover?

The film charts Michael Jackson's life from his childhood in Gary, Indiana as the youngest member of the Jackson 5, through his transformation into one of the most globally famous human beings who ever lived, to the controversies, the trial, and ultimately his death in 2009. Given that the film is produced with Estate cooperation, it will inevitably take a sympathetic view of the more controversial chapters of Jackson's life — a fact that has already drawn criticism from some quarters and fierce defence from Jackson's vast global fanbase.

The film's music is one of its undeniable strengths. Jackson's catalogue — Thriller, Billie Jean, Beat It, Man in the Mirror, Black or White, and dozens more — remains among the most recognisable music ever recorded. Hearing these songs in a cinematic context, performed by Jaafar with the full weight of his family history behind him, promises to be a deeply emotional experience regardless of one's views on the biographical framing.

The India Angle: Michael Jackson's Legacy in India

Michael Jackson has one of the most loyal posthumous fanbases in India of any Western artist. His Dangerous World Tour's 1996 India visit remains a legendary cultural event in Indian popular memory. Fan clubs across India, Thriller dance recreations, and a dedicated Indian ARMY of MJ fans who have kept his music alive on streaming platforms — all of this makes Michael one of the most anticipated Hollywood releases of 2026 among Indian audiences. The film is expected to release simultaneously across Indian multiplexes on April 24. Follow HedwigPost for our full review of Michael when it hits screens.

title: Who Is Winning the Streaming Wars in 2026? Netflix Pulls Ahead as Disney+ Fights to Stay Relevant

excerpt: Netflix is dominating 2026 with BTS, Bridgerton and Squid Game 3. Disney Plus is struggling. HBO is fighting back with Euphoria. Here is who is winning the streaming wars in 2026 — and what it means for viewers.
content:
Netflix Is Lapping the Competition

If the streaming wars of 2026 have a clear front-runner, it is Netflix — and it is not particularly close. The platform enters the second quarter of 2026 having scored what may be its most culturally dominant quarter since its early streaming days. Bridgerton Season 4 sat at number one in Netflix's weekly top 10 for four consecutive weeks after its January release. The BTS concert livestream on March 21 reached viewers in 190 countries simultaneously — the first time Netflix had ever globally broadcast a live concert — and the accompanying documentary BTS: THE RETURN premieres March 27. Squid Game Season 3, confirmed for a 2026 release, is one of the most anticipated sequels in streaming history.

Netflix's strategy of investing in live events — including NFL Christmas games, WWE programming, and now the BTS concert — is paying off in subscriber engagement metrics. The platform is also benefiting from its ad-supported tier, which now accounts for over 40% of new sign-ups globally and has given Netflix a powerful new advertising revenue stream that rivals its subscription income in high-growth markets like India.

Disney+ Is Struggling to Find Its Footing

Disney+ enters 2026 in a more difficult position. The platform's subscriber growth has stalled in many markets, and its content strategy — heavily dependent on Marvel and Star Wars sequels that have received increasingly mixed reception from both fans and critics — is being re-evaluated. The announcement that Netflix had acquired a significant stake in Warner Bros. Discovery (pending regulatory approval) spooked Disney executives, who are now facing the prospect of an even larger and more powerful Netflix competing directly for the franchise content that Disney once considered its exclusive domain. Marvel's Phase 6 slate is set to launch on Disney+ in late 2026, and the studio is banking on a narrative reset to re-energise the universe.

In India specifically, Disney+ Hotstar's dominance in cricket — particularly IPL streaming rights — gives it a floor of subscribers that no other platform can easily displace. The IPL 2026 season begins March 28, and Hotstar's IPL viewership in India consistently exceeds 150 million concurrent viewers at peak, a number no entertainment streaming platform in the world comes close to matching.

HBO Max: Quality Over Quantity Is Working

HBO Max is quietly having its best content year in a long time. Euphoria Season 3 lands in April. The Pitt Season 2 and The White Lotus Season 4 are both confirmed for 2026. The network's strategy of releasing fewer shows but making each one an event has given HBO Max a cultural prestige that rivals Netflix's sheer scale. Industry surveys consistently show HBO Max as the platform viewers trust most for quality drama and adult-oriented programming.

What About Indian Viewers? The Best Platforms for India in 2026

For Indian viewers in 2026, the streaming landscape looks like this: Netflix India is the clear choice for global entertainment, Korean content, and premium originals. Disney+ Hotstar remains essential for cricket, especially IPL, and for a broad catalogue of Bollywood and Hollywood titles. Amazon Prime Video India is strong for regional Indian content, particularly Telugu and Malayalam cinema. SonyLIV is the destination for cricket's ICC tournaments and select Bollywood originals. JioCinema, having secured some major sports rights, is a growing challenger. Our recommendation: Netflix plus one sports-focused platform (Hotstar or JioCinema) covers 90% of what most Indian viewers want. title: How K-Pop Conquered India: From Niche Fandom to Mainstream Cultural Force in 2026
author: HedwigPost Editorial
excerpt: India is now one of BTS's top five streaming countries in the world. K-pop is no longer a niche interest in India — it is a mainstream cultural force. Here is how it happened and where it is going.
content:
India's K-Pop Moment Has Arrived

When BTS performed at Seoul's Gwanghwamun Square on March 21, 2026, hundreds of thousands of Indian fans watched the Netflix livestream simultaneously — many gathered in community watch parties in Mumbai, Delhi, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, and Chennai. India does not yet have a K-pop concert tour stop to call its own, but make no mistake: India is now among the top five countries in the world for BTS streaming, and K-pop's penetration of the Indian youth market has become one of the most significant entertainment industry stories of the decade.

A decade ago, K-pop was essentially unknown in India outside a small, intensely devoted fandom concentrated in urban metros. Today, it is a mainstream cultural reference point for tens of millions of young Indians between the ages of 13 and 28. How did this transformation happen so completely, and so quickly?

The Gateway Drug: K-Dramas and YouTube

The K-pop explosion in India tracks directly with the rise of K-drama consumption, driven by Netflix and YouTube. Shows like Crash Landing on You, Squid Game, My Love from the Star, and more recently The Glory and Lovely Runner have given Indian audiences a window into Korean storytelling, visual aesthetics, and emotional sensibilities that resonated deeply — particularly with young women. K-drama fans became curious about the music their favourite actors starred in or that featured on drama soundtracks. BTS's presence on YouTube — with music videos that regularly exceeded 100 million views — provided an accessible, high-quality entry point. The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated everything: bored, homebound young people had unlimited time to tumble down the K-pop rabbit hole on YouTube and social media.

What Makes Indian ARMY Different

Indian BTS fans — who identify proudly as ARMY — have built one of the most organised and vocal fan communities in any country. Indian ARMY regularly trend BTS hashtags to the top of India's Twitter and Instagram charts, organise charity drives in BTS members' names, and create high-quality fan art, fan fiction, and video edits that circulate globally. The community spans languages — Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Bengali, Malayalam — making it one of the few truly pan-India youth cultural phenomena of the current era.

The hunger for a BTS concert in India is palpable and vocal. Fan petitions requesting India dates on the Arirang World Tour gathered hundreds of thousands of signatures within hours of the tour announcement. Industry analysts at Live Nation India have described an India date as "commercially inevitable" given the demand — the question is timing, venue capacity, and the logistical complexity of staging a production of this scale in India.

Beyond BTS: The Full K-Pop Ecosystem Taking Root in India

K-pop's Indian expansion is not a single-artist story. BLACKPINK, TWICE, SEVENTEEN, STRAY KIDS, and newer fourth-generation groups including TOMORROW X TOGETHER, ENHYPEN, and NewJeans all have significant and growing Indian fanbases. Lollapalooza India 2025 featured K-pop acts for the first time, and industry observers expect K-pop acts to become a regular fixture on the Indian festival and concert circuit. K-drama streaming hours in India on Netflix grew 40% year-over-year in 2025. Korean food delivery orders in major Indian cities are up 150% over three years, according to Zomato data. K-beauty products are now stocked in major Indian retail chains. The Korean Wave — Hallyu — has arrived in India, and it shows no signs of receding. title: Euphoria Season 3 Is Almost Here: Release Date, Cast, Plot Details and What the Five-Year Time Jump Means
author: HedwigPost Editorial
excerpt: Euphoria Season 3 is finally coming to HBO Max in April 2026, four years after Season 2. Zendaya, Sydney Sweeney and Jacob Elordi return — and Cassie and Nate get married. Here's everything we know.
content:
The Four-Year Wait Is Almost Over

Euphoria Season 3 arrives on HBO Max in April 2026 — four years after the polarising but culturally dominant second season aired in 2022. The wait has been one of the most discussed hiatuses in prestige television history, driven partly by the 2023 writers' and actors' strikes, partly by the challenge of scheduling a cast whose profiles have exploded since Season 2 aired, and partly by creator-showrunner Sam Levinson's determination to get the season right rather than simply get it out. By all accounts, the wait has been worth it.

HBO released its first full trailer for Season 3 in February 2026, and social media went into immediate meltdown. Clips of Zendaya's Rue, noticeably older and visibly different from where we left her in 2022, circulated millions of times in the first 24 hours. The show's fashion, cinematography, and soundtrack choices — even in the trailer — prompted the same level of intense cultural commentary that made Euphoria one of the defining TV shows of its era.

The Five-Year Time Jump: Where Is Everyone Now?

Season 3 features a significant five-year time jump from where Season 2 ended. Creator Sam Levinson has been deliberately sparse with plot details, but several key character updates have been confirmed or strongly signalled. Rue (Zendaya) begins the season in Mexico, having crossed the border in search of what Levinson describes as "innovative ways" to deal with her ongoing debt to drug dealer Laurie. Cassie (Sydney Sweeney) and Nate (Jacob Elordi) are married — a development that will undoubtedly provide the season with its most explosive domestic drama. Jules (Hunter Schafer) is studying at art school. Maddie (Alexa Demie) works at a Hollywood talent agency. Lexi (Maude Apatow) is a writer's assistant to a showrunner played by Sharon Stone.

The five-year jump allows the show to do something that Season 2's compressed timeline prevented: let the characters inhabit fully adult situations with fully adult consequences. They are no longer protected by the relative safety of high school — the choices they make now are permanent in a way they never were before. This thematic shift appears to be at the heart of what Levinson is exploring in Season 3.

Why Euphoria Still Matters in 2026

In the four years since Season 2, the cultural landscape around Euphoria has shifted considerably. The debate about whether the show glorifies or honestly depicts substance abuse, trauma, and adolescent chaos has not gone away — if anything, with a more mature cast playing post-college characters, it will intensify. But Euphoria's visual grammar — its operatic cinematography, its use of music as emotional architecture, its refusal of conventional TV narrative structure — remains genuinely unlike anything else on television. The show created a generation of viewers who experience pop culture more intensely because of it.

title: Dhurandhar 2 Box Office Collection: Ranveer Singh's Spy Thriller Makes History With Rs. 339 Crore in 3 Days
author: HedwigPost Editorial

excerpt: Dhurandhar 2: The Revenge starring Ranveer Singh has crossed Rs. 339 crore in just 3 days, becoming the first Bollywood film to score Rs. 100 crore net in Hindi in a single day. Full box office collection here.
content:
The Biggest Bollywood Blockbuster of 2026 Has Arrived

Director Aditya Dhar's spy action thriller Dhurandhar 2: The Revenge has set Bollywood on fire in its opening weekend. Starring Ranveer Singh in what critics are calling the finest performance of his career, the film opened on March 20, 2026 with advance booking earnings of Rs. 43 crore on Day 0 — before it had even officially released. On its first official day of release (Day 1, Thursday), the film crossed Rs. 102.55 crore net — making it the first Hindi film in Bollywood history to earn Rs. 100 crore net on a single day. By the end of its third day (Saturday), the cumulative total had reached Rs. 339.27 crore in India alone.

Worldwide, the film crossed Rs. 550 crore in just three days, with the overseas collection contributing Rs. 149.65 crore. In Australia alone, the film smashed AUD 1 million on a single day — a benchmark for Indian cinema in the region. The numbers have sent the entire Indian film industry into celebratory overdrive.

Day-Wise Box Office Collection

Day 0 (Wednesday — advance/preview shows): Rs. 43 crore (Hindi only). Day 1 (Thursday): Rs. 102.55 crore total (Hindi: Rs. 99.1 crore; Telugu: Rs. 2.12 crore; Tamil: Rs. 1.16 crore; Kannada and Malayalam making up the rest). Day 2 (Friday): Rs. 80.72 crore (slight dip typical of post-opening Friday adjustment). Day 3 (Saturday): Rs. 113 crore (massive 40% jump on Saturday — the single biggest day for Hindi cinema in 2026). Cumulative 3-day total: Rs. 339.27 crore net (India) / Rs. 550 crore worldwide.

What Is Dhurandhar 2 About?

Dhurandhar 2: The Revenge is the sequel to the 2024 original, with Ranveer Singh returning as the super-spy protagonist in a story that director Aditya Dhar has described as larger in both scale and emotional depth than the first film. SS Rajamouli, one of Bollywood's most respected voices, posted his praise on social media: "Dhurandhar-1 was great, but The Revenge surpassed the original in both scale and soul. The writing, casting, technical execution, music, world design and direction are flawless. But it's the emotional stakes that really ground it." Allu Arjun called it "a film that will make every patriot proud" while Mahesh Babu described it as "the finest version of Ranveer unleashed."

The film's music has also become a viral sensation. The song "Aari Aari" — a remake of Bombay Rockers' iconic track — has become a social media phenomenon, with fan videos accumulating millions of views across Instagram and YouTube Shorts.

A New Era for Bollywood?

Dhurandhar 2's performance is significant beyond just the numbers. After years of debate about whether Bollywood could match South Indian cinema's commercial dominance, the film represents a clear statement that pan-India blockbusters can originate from Hindi cinema too. The film performed strongly in Telugu and Tamil markets — a testament to Ranveer Singh's star power cutting across regional boundaries. For fans waiting for news on upcoming major Bollywood releases, Shah Rukh Khan's highly anticipated "King" is slated for December 2026. title: Bridgerton Season 4 Review: Benedict and Sophie's Cinderella Romance Is the Ton's Best Yet
author: HedwigPost Editorial
excerpt: Bridgerton Season 4 is now fully streaming on Netflix. Benedict's Cinderella romance with Sophie is here — find out what happened, who's new in the cast, and what Season 5 and 6 will bring.
content:
The Wait Is Over: Benedict's Story Is Finally Here

After nearly two years since Season 3's emotional Colin-and-Penelope conclusion, Netflix has delivered Bridgerton Season 4 in full — Parts 1 and 2 dropped on January 29 and February 26, 2026 respectively. The new season adapts the third novel in Julia Quinn's beloved Regency romance series, An Offer from a Gentleman, casting the Bridgerton family's second son Benedict as the protagonist at last. For fans who have been waiting since Season 1 for the bohemian, artistic Benedict to get his moment in the sun, Season 4 delivers everything they hoped for and then some.

British-born actor Luke Thompson, who has been building a fanbase since Season 1, is extraordinary in the lead role. He brings a wounded vulnerability and genuine intellectual depth to Benedict that makes his romantic journey feel far more emotionally complex than the classic Cinderella template might suggest. Korean-Australian actress Yerin Ha is equally compelling as Sophie Baek, a resourceful lady's maid who catches Benedict's eye at Lady Violet's masquerade ball — and who struggles, throughout both parts of the season, between her heart's desires and the harsh practical realities of 19th century class society.

The Cinderella Story With a Class-Conscious Twist

What makes Season 4 stand out from its predecessors is how seriously showrunner Jess Brownell takes the class politics underlying the Cinderella structure. "Benedict lives in a fantasy world. Sophie lives in a hard reality," Brownell has said in interviews. This tension — between romantic idealism and material reality — gives the season a weight that the earlier, glossier seasons sometimes lacked. Sophie is not simply waiting to be rescued; she is actively managing her own survival, her own dignity, and her own dreams in a world that has very little room for any of them. The series never lets us forget the labour that underpins the Bridgerton household's effortless elegance.

The masquerade ball of Part 1's finale — in which Benedict falls for the mysterious Lady in Silver without realising she is the very maid he has already befriended — is one of the most beautifully staged sequences in the entire series. And when the reveal comes, the emotional fallout is handled with a sophistication that had fans immediately clamouring for Part 2.

What's New in the Cast?

Season 4 introduces several new faces to the ton. Yerin Ha (known for her role in Halo) is the biggest new addition as Sophie. The season also sees Claudia Jessie's Eloise take a more prominent supporting role as Benedict's reluctant co-conspirator — and as the Bridgerton sibling most visibly being left behind by her family's romantic adventures. Julie Andrews returns as the voice of Lady Whistledown, providing the narration that ties the season together with characteristic dry wit.

Renewed for Seasons 5 and 6: What Comes Next?

Netflix has already confirmed that Bridgerton will continue for Seasons 5 and 6, meaning the entire eight-sibling family saga is set to conclude on screen. Season 5 is expected to follow Eloise's story, as per Julia Quinn's novel To Sir Phillip, With Love. Season 6 will likely focus on youngest sister Hyacinth. With Benedict and Sophie's story now complete, the Ton has five more Bridgertons waiting for their happily ever afters. title: Oscars 2026: "One Battle After Another" Wins Best Picture — The Complete Winners List and Biggest Moments
author: HedwigPost Editorial
excerpt: One Battle After Another won Best Picture at the 98th Academy Awards, while Sinners made history with 16 nominations. Here is the complete winners list, the biggest moments, and the surprising upsets from Oscars night.
content:
Best Picture Goes to "One Battle After Another"

Paul Thomas Anderson's "One Battle After Another" took home the biggest prize at the 98th Academy Awards on March 15, 2026, winning Best Picture in what was ultimately a dramatic six-award sweep. The film — a political thriller set in a police state version of America — also won Best Director, Best Adapted Screenplay, and Best Film Editing for Anderson, plus Best Supporting Actor for Sean Penn (who famously did not attend) and the first-ever Oscar for Best Casting, awarded to Cassandra Kulukundis. Anderson, receiving his first Oscar wins after more than 30 years of acclaimed filmmaking, thanked his children during his screenplay acceptance speech: "I wrote this movie for my kids to say sorry for the housekeeping mess that we left in this world we're handing off to them."

"Sinners" Made History — Just Not the Kind Anyone Expected

Ryan Coogler's Sinners arrived at the 98th Oscars carrying the most nominations in Academy Awards history — a staggering 16 nods, surpassing the previous records held by Titanic, All About Eve, and La La Land. It left with four Oscars — Best Actor for Michael B. Jordan, Best Original Screenplay for Coogler, Best Original Score for Ludwig Göransson, and Best Cinematography for Autumn Durald Arkapaw. Arkapaw's win was historic: she became the first woman ever to win the Academy Award for Best Cinematography.

The twelve losses mean Sinners now holds a different record — the most nominations to losses in Oscar history. The previous record of 11 losses was shared by five films going back to 1948. For Coogler, who coaxed his entire cast to stand for applause when he collected his screenplay award, the four wins clearly meant something deep. Michael B. Jordan, accepting his first Oscar for playing twins Smoke and Stack, recited from memory a list of previous Black Best Actor winners, honouring the "ancestors" whose legacy he was proud to extend.

Complete Winners List

Best Picture: One Battle After Another. Best Director: Paul Thomas Anderson (One Battle After Another). Best Actor: Michael B. Jordan (Sinners). Best Actress: Jessie Buckley (Hamnet). Best Supporting Actor: Sean Penn (One Battle After Another). Best Supporting Actress: Amy Madigan (Weapons). Best Animated Feature: KPop Demon Hunters. Best Original Song: "Golden" from KPop Demon Hunters — the first K-pop song ever to win an Oscar. Best International Feature Film: Sentimental Value (Norway). Best Documentary Feature: Mr. Nobody Against Putin. Best Original Screenplay: Ryan Coogler for Sinners. Best Adapted Screenplay: Paul Thomas Anderson for One Battle After Another. Best Original Score: Ludwig Göransson for Sinners. Best Cinematography: Sinners (Autumn Durald Arkapaw — first woman ever). Best Film Editing: One Battle After Another (Andy Jurgensen). Best Casting (inaugural award): Cassandra Kulukundis for One Battle After Another. Best Live Action Short Film: Tie — "The Singers" and "Two People Exchanging Saliva" — only the seventh tie in Oscars history.

The Ceremony: Political, Emotional, and Occasionally Chaotic

Conan O'Brien returned as host for the second consecutive year, opening with an extended video parody that saw him chased through scenes from Oscar-nominated films by a group of schoolchildren. The ceremony was held under unusually heavy security — FBI alerts of a possible Iranian drone attack on California following the US-Iran war meant police dogs were visible on the red carpet and helicopters circled overhead throughout the night. The political atmosphere was palpable on stage: presenter Javier Bardem used his moment to say "No to war and free Palestine" while presenting the Best International Feature award; Jimmy Kimmel mocked President Trump from the stage; and winning documentary filmmakers used their acceptance speeches for pointed political statements. The night's most moving moment came in the In Memoriam segment, paying tribute to Rob Reiner, Robert Redford, Diane Keaton, and Catherine O'Hara.

The Most Anticipated Comeback in Music History

On March 21, 2026, BTS made history for the second time in a single weekend — following the release of their new album Arirang on March 20, the group performed their first full concert in nearly four years at Gwanghwamun Square in central Seoul, South Korea. An estimated 260,000 fans packed the historic square — the largest gathering in the city for a K-pop concert ever recorded. The event was simultaneously live-streamed on Netflix to viewers in 190 countries, making it the first time the streaming giant had globally broadcast a live concert.

For BTS fans, known worldwide as ARMY, the weekend was the culmination of three and a half years of waiting. In 2022, BTS announced an indefinite hiatus as its members — RM, Jin, SUGA, j-hope, Jimin, V, and Jung Kook — began fulfilling South Korea's mandatory military service requirement. The final member, SUGA, completed his service in June 2025. The group had quietly reunited in a Los Angeles recording studio shortly after, spending July to November 2025 recording what would become Arirang.

Arirang: The Album That Reclaims Their Roots

Titled after Korea's most beloved traditional folk song, Arirang is BTS's fifth Korean-language studio album and their tenth album overall. The 14-track project is widely being described by critics as BTS's most artistically ambitious work since their 2014 breakthrough album Dark & Wild. Rather than chasing the glossy pop crossover sound of chart-toppers like Dynamite and Butter, Arirang leans into hip-hop, spoken word, and experimental sounds that reflect the group's personal growth during their years of military service and separation.

The album sold 3.98 million copies on its very first day — one of the highest first-day sales figures in K-pop history. The music video for the lead single SWIM surpassed 40 million views within 24 hours of release. On the album's first day, BTS's entire back catalogue re-entered streaming charts worldwide as new and returning listeners dove back in. Billboard confirmed the group's first-day numbers as among the highest for any album released in 2026.

"The opening 15 minutes of Arirang have the rebellious, rap-heavy energy of the band's 2014 album, Dark & Wild," wrote the BBC's Mark Savage in a glowing four-star review. "Surefire radio hits, they cemented BTS as the biggest K-pop band on Planet Earth. The good news is the band have rekindled that fire."

The Concert: 260,000 Fans and a Drone Light Show

The one-hour live show, officially titled BTS THE COMEBACK LIVE | ARIRANG, opened with a pre-show drone light show that illuminated the night sky above Seoul with portraits of the seven members. Directed by Hamish Hamilton — the British director responsible for multiple Super Bowl halftime shows and the Oscars — the stage design was built around the concept of a picture frame, set against the backdrop of Gyeongbokgung Palace. The setlist was dominated by new material from Arirang, including the anthemic closing number Into the Sun, during which all seven members shared vocal lines in a display of unity that reduced fans both at the venue and watching online to tears.

Jung Kook's high notes in "Please," Jimin's emotive delivery in "Merry Go Round," and SUGA and j-hope's rap intensity in "Hooligan" were cited by reviewers as the standout individual moments. RM performed despite an ankle injury that had concerned fans in the days leading up to the show. The concert was directed to be streamed on Netflix and will remain available for replay for all subscribers.

The Arirang World Tour: 82 Shows, 34 Regions, April 2026 to March 2027

The Seoul concert was only the beginning. The Arirang World Tour officially kicks off on April 9–12, 2026 in Goyang, South Korea, and spans 82 scheduled dates across Asia, North America, Europe, Latin America, and Australia — all the way through March 2027. Live Nation reported close to 2.4 million tickets sold in the first days of sale, with all North America, Europe, and UK stadium dates already sold out. Analysts at Live Nation are projecting that the tour could rival Taylor Swift's record-breaking Eras Tour as the most commercially successful concert tour of all time.

Indian ARMY take note: no India dates have been confirmed in the initial tour announcement, but given the enormous fanbase in India — consistently one of the top five countries for BTS streaming — the group's management at HYBE has not ruled out additional Asian dates being announced. Directed by Bao Nguyen (The Greatest Night in Pop), the documentary BTS: THE RETURN premieres on Netflix on March 27, 2026. The film follows the seven members through the creation of Arirang, offering rare behind-the-scenes access to their reunion, their military experiences, and their creative process. title: Beyond the Headlines: The Human Cost of the Iran War That the World Cannot Afford to Forget
content:
The Numbers Behind the Conflict

News coverage of the Iran war is dominated by military movements, oil prices, and diplomatic manoeuvring. But behind all of it is a human story of extraordinary suffering. According to Al Jazeera's confirmed casualty tracker as of March 22, the war has killed at least 1,444 people in Iran — including at least 204 children. At least 18 people have been killed in Israel by Iranian missile and drone strikes. Thirteen US service members have died, along with six additional crew members killed when a US refuelling aircraft crashed in western Iraq. At least 21 people have been killed in Gulf states — Bahrain, Kuwait, Jordan, and others — as Iranian attacks spread across the region.

These numbers are preliminary and likely to be significantly undercounted. Iran's media environment is heavily restricted during the conflict, and access for independent journalists is extremely limited. The real toll on Iranian civilians — killed by direct strikes, by the disruption of medical supply chains, or by the collapse of basic infrastructure — may not be known for months or years.

A New Year Under Fire: Nowruz and Eid in Wartime

The timing of the conflict has added a particularly painful cultural dimension for Iranians. March 2026 saw the rare alignment of two major holidays — Eid al-Fitr, the feast marking the end of Ramadan, and Nowruz, the Persian New Year celebrated by Iranians worldwide as the most important holiday of the year. Millions of Iranians gathered at holy sites including the Imam Reza Shrine in Mashhad to mark these occasions. Air defences were activated over Tehran on the first day of Nowruz as explosions were heard across the capital. Haft-sin tables — the traditional new year arrangements of symbolic items — stood in homes across Iran as bombs fell outside.

UNESCO World Heritage Sites in the Crossfire

The war has also inflicted damage on some of humanity's most irreplaceable cultural heritage. On March 2, a strike on Arg Square in Tehran damaged the nearby Golestan Palace, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. On March 9, strikes on the city of Isfahan damaged Naqsh-e Jahan Square, Chehel Sotoun, Ali Qapu Palace, the Shah Mosque, and the Jameh Mosque — all globally significant examples of Persian Islamic architecture. The Azadi Sport Complex in Tehran was bombed on March 5. On March 8, the Falak-ol-Aflak fortress, marked with a blue shield emblem signifying its protected cultural heritage status, sustained damage.

UNESCO issued a statement urging the protection of Iran's heritage sites, noting that sites marked with the blue shield — a symbol meant to invoke the same protection as the Red Cross for medical facilities — were being struck nonetheless. The damage to these sites is not simply an aesthetic loss. These are among the great monuments of human civilisation, irreplaceable repositories of art, architecture, and history that have survived for centuries. Their destruction erases something that belongs not just to Iran but to all of humanity.

A Conflict With No Quick End in Sight

As the war enters its fourth week, there is no ceasefire in sight. Trump says the US is considering "winding down" operations, but simultaneously threatening to escalate against Iranian power plants. Israel continues striking Tehran. Iran continues launching missiles at Gulf states and commercial shipping. The Strait of Hormuz remains largely closed. And behind all the geopolitical manoeuvring, ordinary people — Iranian families sheltering from airstrikes, Gulf workers caught in retaliatory attacks, American service members deployed far from home — are paying the heaviest price.

The world's attention is stretched between the geopolitics, the oil prices, and the stock markets. But the human beings at the centre of this conflict deserve to be seen and counted. Their lives and suffering are not a footnote to the economic story. They are the story.

title: Britain Lets the US Use Its Bases, Trump Calls NATO "Cowards": How the West Is Fracturing Over the Iran War
content:
Britain's Controversial Decision

On March 1, 2026 — just three days into the war — UK Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer announced that the United States could use British military bases for what he described as a "specific and limited defensive purpose": to destroy Iranian missiles at source. The BBC confirmed that the bases being made available were Diego Garcia in the British Indian Ocean Territory and RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, England. UK bases on Cyprus were specifically excluded. Starmer was careful to state that Britain itself was not participating militarily in the strikes and that he did "not believe in regime change from the skies" — but the decision to grant the US use of British territory for offensive operations generated significant parliamentary controversy.

The British government published summary legal advice justifying the decision on self-defence grounds, following reports that Iranian ballistic missiles had struck Diego Garcia itself — a UK territory — in the early days of the conflict. The RAF also engaged in limited defensive operations to intercept Iranian missiles, which the government described as acts of self-defence rather than offensive participation.

France, Germany, and the European Position

France and Germany, alongside the UK Prime Minister, issued a joint statement on February 28 condemning Iran's counter-strikes and calling for a "resumption of diplomacy." The statement called on Iran to end its nuclear programme, curtail its ballistic missile programme, stop repressing Iranian citizens, and cease supporting armed groups abroad. Notably, the three European leaders stopped short of endorsing the strikes themselves — the French and German governments were not informed in advance of the US-Israeli operation.

This put European nations in an awkward diplomatic position: opposing Iran's counter-strikes while declining to explicitly support the military operation that provoked them. The EU as a body called for an immediate ceasefire, putting it at odds with Washington's position that no ceasefire agreement would be reached.

Trump's "Cowards" Comment and NATO's Dilemma

As the war entered its fourth week, President Trump publicly berated NATO allies — without naming specific countries — as "cowards" for refusing to help the United States secure the Strait of Hormuz from Iranian attacks on shipping. Trump suggested that nations that use the Strait as a shipping lane should bear responsibility for policing it. The comment reflected a broader frustration in Washington that the military and economic burden of the conflict was falling disproportionately on the United States and Israel. Most NATO members — wary of the alliance's defensive mandate being used to justify offensive operations in the Middle East — declined to commit forces.

The Iran war has revealed genuine fractures within the Western alliance. The question of how far NATO's mutual defence commitments extend — and whether a US president can characterise unilateral offensive operations as defensive — will likely shape Western security architecture for years to come, regardless of how this specific conflict resolves.

title: The Federal Reserve's Iran War Problem: Why Rate Cuts Are Dead and a Hike Is Back on the Table
content:
The Rate Cut That Will Not Come

At the start of 2026, the consensus on Wall Street was clear: the Federal Reserve would cut interest rates two to three times during the year. Inflation was running at 2.4% in January — approaching the Fed's 2% target. The job market was healthy. The economic trajectory was positive. Rate cuts were not a question of "if" but "when." Then February 28 arrived. Within three weeks of the US and Israel striking Iran, those rate cut expectations had been almost entirely cancelled, according to CME Group data tracking fed funds futures markets. Some participants were now pricing in a small but nonzero probability of a rate hike — something that would have seemed absurd before the war.

Why the Iran War Changes the Fed's Calculus Completely

The Federal Reserve faces an extremely uncomfortable situation known in economics as a "supply shock" — an external event that simultaneously pushes prices up (inflationary) and slows economic growth (recessionary). When inflation is caused by too much demand, the Fed's standard tool — raising interest rates to cool borrowing and spending — works well. When inflation is caused by a supply disruption like an oil shock, raising rates can still tame prices but does so by deepening the economic slowdown, potentially triggering a recession. Cutting rates, on the other hand, would provide economic relief but risk letting inflation run hotter.

Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller captured the dilemma publicly. Speaking on CNBC, Waller — who dissented from the majority at January's meeting by voting for a rate cut — said that the longer the war goes on and the higher oil prices remain, "the more inflation is a concern." Treasury yields tell the same story: the 10-year Treasury yield jumped from 3.97% before the war to 4.38% within three weeks, a significant move in the bond market that directly translates into higher mortgage rates and borrowing costs.

What This Means for Your Money

For homebuyers: mortgage rates, which had been gradually declining, are now rising again. For existing homeowners with fixed-rate mortgages, there is no immediate impact. For those with variable-rate products or upcoming refinancing needs, the trajectory is unfavourable. For savers: higher yields on Treasury bonds and money market accounts mean better returns on safe savings vehicles. For investors: higher rates reduce the attractiveness of equities, particularly growth stocks with valuations dependent on low discount rates.

The economy's trajectory in 2026 now depends heavily on one variable: how long the Iran conflict lasts. A resolution within the next month, combined with a reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, would likely allow oil prices to normalise and rate cut expectations to partially recover. A war that drags into summer at current intensity would, according to most independent forecasters, tip the US into technical recession by the fourth quarter of 2026.

title: The Hidden Crisis Inside the Iran War: How It Is Threatening the Food on Your Plate
content:
The Strait of Hormuz Is Also a Food Supply Lane

The world understands by now that the Strait of Hormuz is critical for oil. What receives far less attention is that the same waterway is a critical artery for global food production. The Fertilizer Institute has warned that approximately 50% of global urea and sulfur exports — two of the most important fertilizer inputs — transit through the Strait of Hormuz. Additionally, 20% of global liquefied natural gas, which is a key feedstock for nitrogen fertilizers, passes through the same channel. Without nitrogen fertilizers, crop yields for wheat, rice, corn, and other staple crops fall dramatically.

The UN World Food Programme and multiple independent economic analysts have warned that the war is driving significant, long-term increases in global food prices. The IEA has described the situation as the "greatest global energy and food security challenge in history" — a striking statement from the body that monitors energy markets worldwide.

Who Is Most Vulnerable?

The countries most immediately at risk are those that are simultaneously dependent on Middle Eastern energy imports and already experiencing food insecurity. Sub-Saharan Africa, South and Southeast Asia, and parts of Latin America top this list. According to analysts at the UN World Food Programme, the disruption to fertilizer supply chains echoes the 2022 food crisis triggered by Russia's invasion of Ukraine, which caused wheat and sunflower oil prices to surge and contributed to famine conditions in multiple countries. This crisis has the potential to be worse: the Strait of Hormuz disruption affects a broader basket of agricultural inputs than the Ukraine war did.

Supermarket Prices: What Comes Next

For consumers in developed countries, the impact will be felt more gradually but is no less real. The transmission mechanism runs from oil prices to transport costs, from transport costs to manufacturing costs, and from manufacturing costs to supermarket shelf prices. A 50% increase in the price of urea fertilizer — which farmers buy months before planting — does not show up in bread prices immediately, but it does show up in next season's harvest. Economists are warning that the food price spike triggered by the Iran war could persist for one to two years after the conflict itself ends, due to these agricultural supply chain lags.

The message from every major food security institution is consistent: the Iran war is not just a military and energy crisis. It is a food crisis in slow motion, and the world should be preparing accordingly.

title: El Niño Is Coming Back in 2026 — And Scientists Say It Could Be a Strong One
content:
What Is El Niño and Why Does It Matter?

El Niño is a natural climate pattern characterised by the warming of surface waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean. When it occurs, it disrupts the normal flow of the east-to-west trade winds, spreading warmth across the tropical Pacific and altering weather patterns across the entire globe. The effects are far-reaching: El Niño typically brings severe droughts to Australia and Southeast Asia, heavier rainfall and flooding to parts of the United States and East Africa, warmer winters in Canada and northern Europe, and intensified hurricane activity in the eastern Pacific.

NOAA's Warning: El Niño Likely to Form in 2026

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) issued an advisory confirming that El Niño is likely to form during the summer months of 2026 and persist through the end of the year — and potentially longer. The agency assessed a 1-in-3 chance of it becoming a "strong" El Niño event by winter 2026. This represents a significant upward revision from earlier forecasts, which had suggested only a modest event might develop.

The timing is particularly concerning. The two most recent El Niño events — in 2014–16 and 2023–24 — both brought record heat around the world that fuelled further global temperature increases. The 2023–24 event contributed directly to 2024 becoming the hottest year in recorded history. A new strong El Niño layered on top of the background warming already baked into the climate system could push 2026 or 2027 to break that record again.

What Does This Mean for the Rest of 2026?

For the United States, an El Niño summer typically brings above-average temperatures across most of the country, more active hurricane seasons in the eastern Pacific, and drought conditions across parts of the northern Plains and Pacific Northwest. For Asia, which is already struggling with disrupted energy supplies due to the Iran war, El Niño could deepen drought conditions that threaten rice and wheat harvests. For Sub-Saharan Africa, it brings an increased risk of drought in some regions and flooding in others.

Climate scientists note that the combination of human-caused background warming and natural El Niño variability creates a multiplicative effect on extreme weather events. In plain terms: when El Niño arrives on top of a planet that is already 1.3°C warmer than pre-industrial times, the most extreme heat events, droughts, and rainfall events all become worse than they would be from either factor alone.

What Can You Do to Prepare?

Individuals and households can take practical steps to prepare for an El Niño year: stock emergency water supplies if you live in a drought-prone area, review your home insurance coverage for flood risk, avoid planting drought-sensitive crops during periods of El Niño uncertainty, and stay informed through official NOAA and local meteorological service updates throughout the year.

title: "Virtually Impossible Without Climate Change": The Record March Heat Wave Baking the US in 2026
content:
A Heat Wave That Should Not Exist in March

While a war rages in the Middle East, a different kind of emergency is unfolding across the American Southwest. Beginning in the second week of March 2026, a heat dome of extraordinary power parked itself over the region, driving temperatures 25 to 30 degrees Fahrenheit above average for this time of year. On March 20, Yuma, Arizona, hit 109 degrees Fahrenheit — shattering the previous all-time US March heat record set in Texas in 1954. A nearby temporary weather station recorded 112 degrees Fahrenheit, which would make it the hottest March temperature in US history if confirmed.

In Phoenix, the mercury hit 105°F, breaking the city's all-time March heat record of 100°F set 38 years ago. More than 100 all-time March record highs were broken or tied across California, Arizona, Colorado, Idaho, South Dakota, and Wyoming. Colorado's state climatologist Russ Schumacher called the heat dome "astonishing" for its intensity in March. Other meteorologists described it as "genuinely startling" and "mind-boggling" on social media.

The Science: Climate Change Made This Happen

On March 20, the World Weather Attribution research group published a rapid analysis of the heat wave and reached an unambiguous conclusion: this extreme heat event "would be virtually impossible for this time of year in a world without human-induced climate change." Global temperatures have risen by approximately 1.3 degrees Celsius since preindustrial times, but the American Southwest is warming faster than most regions. The analysis found that the warming "long tail" of the climate spectrum — meaning the most extreme heat episodes — can now exceed the average warming by a substantial margin.

The numbers at a societal level are stark. The area of the US hit by extreme weather in the past five years has doubled compared to 20 years ago. The US is breaking 77% more hot weather records now than in the 1970s. The number and average cost of inflation-adjusted billion-dollar weather disasters in recent years is twice as high as a decade ago and nearly four times higher than 30 years ago. "The clearest signal isn't the science debate. It's insurers walking away," said Craig Fugate, former FEMA director.

The Human Impact: Who Is Most at Risk?

Extreme heat is the deadliest form of extreme weather in the United States — killing more than twice as many people each year as hurricanes and tornadoes combined. Meteorologists warned specifically that the early, unseasonable nature of this heat wave is particularly dangerous because populations have had no time to acclimatise to summer-level temperatures. Elderly people, outdoor workers, and those without access to air conditioning face the greatest risk. Trail closures at Camelback Mountain in Phoenix and other popular outdoor sites were put in place throughout the week.

With El Niño forecast to return in 2026 — which historically drives further global temperature increases — climate scientists warn that events like this March heat wave will become more frequent and more severe. The science is clear: this is what a warming planet looks like.

title: $112 Oil and $4 Gas: How the Iran War Is Hitting Your Wallet and When It Might Stop
content:
From $70 to $112: Oil's Dramatic Six-Week Journey

Before the US and Israel struck Iran on February 28, Brent crude was trading at approximately $70 per barrel — a relatively stable, moderate price that had economists feeling cautiously optimistic about inflation in 2026. Within three weeks, that price had surged to $112.19 per barrel. In the first week of March alone, US crude jumped 20% and Brent rose 17%. Goldman Sachs suggested the elevated prices could last all the way through 2027 if the conflict remained unresolved. Analysts at Capital Economics projected that a prolonged war could push Brent to an average of $150 per barrel over the next six months.

Gas Prices, Mortgage Rates, Grocery Bills: The Domino Effect

Every American has felt the war's impact directly. Gasoline spending in the second week of March was up more than 14% year-over-year, according to Bank of America Institute data — meaning a larger slice of every household budget is now going straight to the gas station. California prices surged above $5 per gallon. Nationally, prices crossed $4 per gallon for the first time since late 2023.

The inflationary pressure is spreading beyond fuel. Higher oil prices raise the cost of producing and transporting almost everything — food, manufactured goods, medicines. The consumer price index was running at 2.4% in January. Economists warn that the oil shock could push inflation well above 3% by summer. And when inflation rises, so do mortgage rates: the yield on the 10-year US Treasury jumped from 3.97% before the war to 4.38% by March 20 — a meaningful increase that translates directly into higher monthly payments for anyone buying a home or refinancing.

Will the Fed Raise Interest Rates?

Before the war, the Federal Reserve was widely expected to cut interest rates in 2026. Now, according to CME Group data, those bets have been almost entirely cancelled. Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller, speaking on CNBC, said the longer the war goes on and the higher oil prices remain, "the more inflation is a concern." Some market participants are even pricing in a small probability of a rate hike — something that would have been unthinkable in January. University of Michigan consumer sentiment surveys taken after February 28 showed a sharp deterioration, completely erasing the improvement recorded before the war started.

The key variable for your wallet is time. A short conflict of two to four weeks — what Trump seems to be aiming for — would likely produce a quick reversal in oil prices and limited lasting damage to household budgets. A prolonged conflict lasting three months or more at current intensity could genuinely push the US into a recession, according to independent economists. title: The Strait of Hormuz Is Closed: Why This 21-Mile Waterway Controls the World's Economy
content:
The Most Important 21 Miles of Water on Earth

The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow waterway — just 21 miles wide at its narrowest point — separating Iran to the north from Oman and the United Arab Emirates to the south. Despite its modest size, no body of water on Earth has more economic significance. Roughly 20% of the world's oil supply passes through this chokepoint every single day, along with approximately 20% of global liquefied natural gas (LNG). For Asia — which depends on Middle Eastern energy to power its economies — the numbers are even more stark: China, India, Japan, and South Korea together account for nearly 70% of the oil that transits the Strait.

"We have not seen anything like this in pretty much the history of the Strait of Hormuz," said Claudio Galimberti, chief economist at energy research firm Rystad Energy, describing the effective halt of traffic as unprecedented. Iran had threatened to close the Strait many times over decades of tensions with the West. Now, for the first time in history, it had made good on that threat.

What Does "Effectively Closed" Mean?

Iran has not physically blockaded the Strait with naval vessels — doing so would be an extreme escalation. Instead, the combination of Iranian ballistic missile attacks on commercial vessels, the IRGC's explicit threats to set fire to any ship attempting passage, and the near-total withdrawal of commercial tankers from the waterway has produced the same practical result. By March 4, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency reported the threat level across the Gulf, Strait of Hormuz, and Gulf of Oman as "critical." There had been 21 confirmed attacks on commercial vessels and offshore infrastructure in the first three weeks of the war.

QatarEnergy declared force majeure on all LNG exports after Iranian drones struck its facilities on March 2. Qatar supplies roughly 20% of the world's LNG — the gas used to heat homes and generate electricity across Europe and Asia. European natural gas prices surged more than 20% almost immediately. In the US, gasoline prices at the pump crossed $4 per gallon for the first time since late 2023, with California prices surging above $5 per gallon.

Trump's Ultimatum: Open It or Lose Your Power Plants

On March 20, President Trump issued one of the most dramatic ultimatums of the conflict: Iran must "fully open, without threat" the Strait of Hormuz within 48 hours, or the United States would strike and "obliterate" Iranian power plants, starting with the largest. Trump's post identified the Damavand Combined Cycle Power Plant near Tehran as a likely first target. The US Treasury simultaneously announced a temporary lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil already loaded on tankers — a move described by analysts as paradoxical given that the US is simultaneously at war with Iran, but driven by desperation to cool surging energy prices.

title: Stock Market Meltdown: How the Iran War Is Destroying Portfolios and What Investors Should Do Now
content:
The Numbers Tell a Brutal Story

When the United States and Israel launched airstrikes on Iran on February 28, 2026, financial markets were closed for the weekend. Samsung overhauled the camera lenses for the S26 Ultra, and the results are evident immediately. Low-light photography in particular has made a significant leap. Scenes that produced noisy, blotchy results on the S25 Ultra now come back sharp and detailed with accurate colors and excellent shadow recovery.

The 10x optical zoom is exceptional — reaching subjects at distance with detail that rivals dedicated telephoto cameras. Video recording at 8K has become genuinely practical rather than a spec sheet talking point, with improved stabilization making handheld footage usable without post-processing.

Battery Life: A Mixed Bag

The 5,500mAh battery gets most users through a full day of heavy use, which is the minimum expectation at this price. Wireless charging at 25W remains slower than competitors — OnePlus and Xiaomi are shipping 80W+ wireless charging on flagship devices. The 65W wired charging reaches 50% in about 30 minutes, which is acceptable but not class-leading.

Power users running the AI features heavily will likely need to top up by evening. Anyone with moderate usage will finish the day with charge to spare.

If you're in the Samsung ecosystem, upgrading from anything older than the S24 series is a genuine quality-of-life improvement. For everyone else, this is the phone that makes the strongest case for switching. The price is hard to swallow — but almost nothing it does disappoints.
